item.title: March Madness Upsets
item.dc:creator: Cooper Olney
item.description:
Introduction

The NCAA Men’s Basketball Tournament, commonly known as March Madness, is one of the most widely followed and unpredictable sporting events in the United States. It features 68 teams in a single elimination format, including both nationally recognized programs and lesser-known schools. This structure creates an environment where unexpected outcomes can occur, making the tournament especially exciting for fans filling out brackets. Despite millions of entries each year, no one has ever achieved a perfect bracket.

One of the most defining features of March Madness is the occurrence of upsets, in which a lower seeded teams defeats a higher seeded opponent. In this analysis, an upset is defined as a game where the seed differences is at least three spots. While higher seeded teams are generally expected to perform better, the tournament consistently produces surprising results. Lower seeded teams that make deep runs are often referred to as “Cinderella teams,” and their success is a major reason why March Madness remains so exciting and difficult to predict.

The data used in this analysis comes two datasets sourced from Kaggle: One focused on upset outcomes, and the other contained team level performance metrics. The upset (Upset Seed Info.csv) dataset includes information on the number of upsets in each tournament, the rounds in which they occurred, and the seed matchups involved. The second dataset (DEV _ March Madness.csv) contains a wide range of team statistics, including both on-court performance metrics and off-court characteristics.

Main Research Question: What team characteristics are associated with unexpected success in March Madness?

Overall, while the tournament is inherently unpredictable, this analysis aims to determine whether underlying patterns exist in the teams that achieve unexpected success. These factors motivate a deeper exploration into the statistical and contextual drivers of upsets and Cinderella runs in March Madness.

Visualizations

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
# Loading kaggle datasets
upset_seed_info <- read_csv(here::here("posts/final_blog_post/Upset Seed Info.csv"))

dev <- read_csv(here::here("posts/final_blog_post/DEV _ March Madness.csv"))

Cleaning datasets

Plot 1

upset_summary <- upset_seed_info |> group_by(YEAR) |>
  summarise(num_upsets = n(),
            avg_seed_diff = round(mean(`SEED DIFF`, na.rm=TRUE), 3))

Plot 2

on_court_performance <- dev |> 
  filter(`Post-Season Tournament Sorting Index` == 1) |>
  select(
    Season, `Mapped ESPN Team Name`, Seed, 
    `Net Rating`, `Adjusted Tempo`,
    `Adjusted Offensive Efficiency`, 
    eFGPct, TOPct, ORPct, FTRate, Off3PtFG, FTPct,
    `Adjusted Defensive Efficiency`, DefFT
  ) |>
  mutate(Seed = as.numeric(Seed)) |>
  filter(Seed >= 10)

# write_csv(on_court_performance, "on_court_performance.csv")

# read in manually cleaned data from excel
data <- read_excel(here::here("posts/final_blog_post/on_court_performance.xlsx"))

data <- data |> select(-c(`Avg Possession Length (Offense)`, `Avg Possession Length (Defense)`, Bench)) |>
  relocate(cinderella, .after = Seed) |>
  mutate(cinderella = if_else(cinderella == 1, "Yes", "No"))

# plot dataset
boxplot_data <- data |>
  select(
    cinderella,
    `Net Rating`,
    `Adjusted Offensive Efficiency`,
    `Adjusted Defensive Efficiency`,
    ORPct,
    TOPct,
    `Adjusted Tempo`
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-cinderella, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value")

Plot 3 & 4

off_court_factors <- dev |> filter(`Post-Season Tournament Sorting Index` == 1) |>
  select(
    Season, `Mapped ESPN Team Name`, Seed, `Short Conference Name`,
    AvgHeight, CenterHeight, PFHeight, SFHeight, SGHeight, PGHeight, EffectiveHeight, Experience, `Active Coaching Length` 
         ) |>
  mutate(Seed = as.numeric(Seed)) |>
  filter(Seed >= 10) |>
  filter(Season >= 2007)

# helper datasets
cinderella_var_data <- data |>
  select(Season, `Mapped ESPN Team Name`, cinderella)

off_court_factors <- off_court_factors |>
  left_join(cinderella_var_data, 
            by = c("Season", "Mapped ESPN Team Name"))

power_confs <- c("ACC", "B10", "B12", "SEC", "P12", "BE")

off_court_factors <- off_court_factors |>
  mutate(
    `Active Coaching Length` = na_if(`Active Coaching Length`, "Unknown"),
    `Active Coaching Length` = gsub(" years?| year", "", `Active Coaching Length`),
    `Active Coaching Length` = as.numeric(`Active Coaching Length`),
    conference_type = if_else(
      `Short Conference Name` %in% power_confs, "Power", "Mid-Major"
    )
  )

# plot data
plot3_data <- off_court_factors |>
  select(cinderella, conference_type, Experience, EffectiveHeight) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(cinderella, conference_type),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  )
combined_data <- inner_join(off_court_factors, data, 
                            by = c("Season", "Mapped ESPN Team Name", "Seed", "cinderella"))

scaled_data <- combined_data |>
  mutate(
    NetRating_z = scale(`Net Rating`),
    OffEff_z = scale(`Adjusted Offensive Efficiency`),
    DefEff_z = scale(`Adjusted Defensive Efficiency`),
    Experience_z = scale(Experience),
    EffHeight_z = scale(EffectiveHeight)
  )

avg_cinderella <- scaled_data |>
  filter(cinderella == "Yes") |>
  summarise(
    team = "Avg Cinderella",
    NetRating_z = mean(NetRating_z, na.rm = TRUE),
    OffEff_z = mean(OffEff_z, na.rm = TRUE),
    DefEff_z = mean(DefEff_z, na.rm = TRUE),
    Experience_z = mean(Experience_z, na.rm = TRUE),
    EffHeight_z = mean(EffHeight_z, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

case_teams <- scaled_data |>
  filter(
    (`Mapped ESPN Team Name` == "Davidson" & Season == 2008) |
    (`Mapped ESPN Team Name` == "Saint Peter's" & Season == 2022) |
    (`Mapped ESPN Team Name` == "Loyola Chicago" & Season == 2018)
  ) |>
  select(team = `Mapped ESPN Team Name`, 
         NetRating_z, OffEff_z, DefEff_z, Experience_z, EffHeight_z)

# plot data
plot4_data <- bind_rows(case_teams, avg_cinderella) |>
  pivot_longer(-team, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value")

Plot 1: March Madness Upsets Over Time

ggplot(upset_summary, aes(x = YEAR, y = num_upsets)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = YEAR, xend = YEAR, y = 0, yend = num_upsets,
                   color = avg_seed_diff)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = avg_seed_diff), size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name ="Avg Seed Diff") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "March Madness Upsets Over Time",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Number of Upsets"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(upset_summary$num_upsets),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.5)

From the plot, we can see the number of upsets each year on the y-axis, with years ranging from 2008 to 2025 on the x-axis. The year with the fewest upsets is 2025, while 2014 has the most. The dashed red line represented the average number of upsets across all years in the dataset. In addition to the number of upsets, the color of each point represents the average seed difference in those games. For example, if a 12-seed beats a 5-seed, the seed difference is 7. Based on this, we see larger average seed differences in years like 2021 and 2013, and smaller differences in years like 2025 and 2009.

Looking more closely at 2025, there are not only fewer upsets, but the upsets that do occur tend to have smaller seed differences. Tournaments like this are often described as “chalky,” meaning that the higher seeded teams generally perform as expected. On the other end, years like 2021 and 2022 show both a higher number of upsets and larger seed differences. One possible explanation for this is the impact of COVID-19 on recruiting and player development During this time, recruiting was more limited and disrupted, which may have led to better players ending up at smaller program, so then those smaller teams could be more likely to become Cinderella teams.

Overall, this plot suggest that the number of upsets varies from year to year without a clear trend, which indicated that upset frequency alone may not be enough to explain unexpected success. This reinforces the idea to look deeper into team characteristics.

Plot 2: On-Court Metrics: Cinderella vs Non-Cinderella Teams

ggplot(boxplot_data, aes(x = cinderella, y = value, fill = cinderella)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    title = "On-Court Metrics: Cinderella vs Non-Cinderella Teams",
    x = "Cinderella",
    y = "Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Yes" = "#C3EEFF",
    "No" = "#F88158"
  ))

The plot compares double-digit seeded teams across six difference metrics that are commonly used to evaluate basketball performance. These include metrics such as Adjusted Defensive Efficiency, Adjusted Offensive Efficiency, and Net Rating. Looking at the distributions, Cinderella teams tend to have higher Adjusted Offensive Efficiency and a noticeably higher Net Rating compared to non-Cinderella teams. However, somewhat surprisingly, they appear to have a worse Adjusted Defensive Efficiency. For the remaining metrics, the differences between the two groups are minuscule.

One possible explanation for the higher Net Rating is that Cinderella teams are more likely to come from the stronger end of the double-digit seed range, such as 10, 11, or 12 seeds, rather than 15 or 16 seeds. Since these teams are generally stronger overall, this could help explain their higher Net Rating. More importantly, the results suggest that offensive performance may play a larger role than defense in these unexpected tournament runs. teams that are highly efficient offensively can “get hot” and score at a high level, which is especially impactful in a single elimination setting where one strong performance can be enough to advance. Even if these teams are weaker defensively, a strong offense may allow them to win multiple games.

Overall, this plot suggests that for double-digit seeded teams, offensive strength is more strongly associated with making a Cinderella run than defensive performance.

Plot 3: Average Cinderella Team vs. Case Studies

ggplot(plot4_data, aes(x = metric, y = value, fill = metric)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~team) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Cinderella Team vs. Case Studies",
    x = "",
    y = "Standardized Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d()

The plot includes several of the metrics from the previous plots, such as Adjusted Offensive Efficiency, Adjusted Defensive Efficiency, Net Rating, Effective Height, and Experience. All values are standardized using z-scores, meaning a value of 0 represents the average among all double-digit seeded teams. this allows for direct comparison across teams and metrics. Looking first at the average Cinderella team, the values in this plot generally align with the patterns observed in the previous plots. Showing above average Offensive Efficiency and Net Rating, with moderate differences in other metrics.

Moving to the case studies, each teams tells a slightly different story. Davidson, before the tournament was considered a very strong double-digit seeded team, but now famous because of their star player Stephen Curry. They closely follow the overall Cinderella profile but at a more extreme level. They were significantly above average offensively and below average defensively, reinforcing the idea that strong offensive performance can drive unexpected tournament success. This also supports the perception that Davidson may have been under-seeded as they performed more like a higher-seeded team.

Saint Peter’s, however, stands out as the most unusual case here. As a 15-seed that reached the Elite Eight, they were below average in both offensive and defensive efficiency compared to other double-digit seeded teams. This makes their run especially surprising, as they do not fit the statistical profile associated with most Cinderella teams. Their success highlights how unpredictable the tournament can be, especially in a single elimination format.

Overall, these case studies reinforce the idea that offensively strong teams are more likely to achieve unexpected success in March Madness. However, Saint Peter’s demonstrates that offensive efficiency is not the only path to a Cinderella run. These examples show that while general patterns exist, individual Cinderella runs can vary widely, adding to the unpredictability that defines March Madness.

Conclusion

Overall, this analysis suggests that offensive efficiency is one of the strongest factors associated with unexpected success in March Madness. Among double-digit seeded teams that go on Cinderella runs, those that are more offensively oriented tend to perform better than those that rely primarily on defense. The main takeaway is that teams capable of scoring efficiently and “getting hot” are more likely to achieve unexpected success in a single-elimination setting like March Madness.

There are several limitations to this analysis. The data only covers a relatively recent time period, and only a small subset of the available metrics was used. Other variables could provide stronger explanations for unexpected success but were not explored here.

If given more time, this analysis could be extended by looking deeper into specific offensive metrics could help identify if certain aspects of offense are more important for Cinderella teams. Additionally, other influences to look at could be the more recent changes in college basketball, such as the transfer portal and NIL, as they could also influence the likelihood of upsets in future tournaments.

item.title: Yellowstone Biodiversity
item.dc:creator: Cooper Olney
item.description:
Introduction

The data used in this analysis contains information on species that have been recorded in Yellowstone National Park. The dataset includes details about different organisms found within the park, it contains 4179 observations, each corresponding to a species recorded within the park.

The variables I am most interested in are CategoryName, which represents the type of organism, along with Nativeness, which indicates whether a species is native to the region or not. These variables show how biodiversity in Yellowstone is distributed across different types of organisms and whether most species present in the park are native or non-native.

This leads to my primary question of interest:

What does the composition of species in Yellowstone National Park reveal about the park’s biodiversity and the presence of native vs non-native species?

The data was accessed through the TidyTuesday project on a GitHub repository. The original source of the data can be found [here]. (https://irma.nps.gov/NPSpecies/Search/SpeciesList)

Some additional context about Yellowstone and the National Park system is helpful for interpreting this data. The National Park Service maintains detailed records of species that occur within park boundaries through a combination of field observations, research studies, and verified documentation. These records help scientists and park managers monitor biodiversity and identify potential conservation concerns such as the introduction of non-native species.

Yellowstone National Park is one of the most biologically diverse parks in the United States, containing a wide range of ecosystems including forests, grasslands, rivers, and geothermal areas. Because of this ecological diversity, the park supports thousands of different species across many groups. Understanding how these species are distributed across categories and whether they are native or non-native provides insight into the overall structure of biodiversity within the park.

Primary Visualizations

Setting up the Data

library(tidyverse)
most_visited_nps_species_data <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-10-08/most_visited_nps_species_data.csv')
# Data Prep
 yellowstone_species <- most_visited_nps_species_data |> 
  filter(ParkCode == "YELL")|> 
  select(ParkName, CategoryName, Order, Family, TaxonRecordStatus, CommonNames, ParkAccepted, Sensitive, RecordStatus, Occurrence, Nativeness, Abundance, NPSTags, References, Observations, Vouchers, GRank, SRank)

Plot 1: Species Counts by Category in Yellowstone

category_counts <- yellowstone_species |> count(CategoryName) |>
  mutate(CategoryName = fct_reorder(CategoryName, n))

ggplot(data = category_counts, aes(x = CategoryName, y = n)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = CategoryName, xend = CategoryName, y = 0, yend = n),
               color = "darkgreen") +
  geom_point(color = "darkgreen") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.2, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Species Counts by Category in Yellowstone",
       x = "Species Category",
       y = "Number of Species") +
  theme_minimal()

From the lollipop plot we can see that the majority of species recorded in Yellowstone fall within the insect and vascular plant categories. This makes sense because plants and insects tend to have far more species than larger organisms in most ecosystems. The next largest category is birds, while physically larger groups such as mammals, fish, reptiles, and amphibians contain far fewer species.

These patterns reflect how biodiversity is typically structured in nature. Smaller organisms with many ecological niches, like insects and plants, dominate species counts, while larger organisms make up a smaller portion of total biodiversity. Overall, the plot shows that Yellowstone’s biodiversity is largely driven by plant and insect species.

Plot 2: Nativeness of Species Across Categories

heatmap_data <- yellowstone_species |> count(CategoryName, Nativeness)
  
ggplot(data = heatmap_data, aes(x = Nativeness, y = CategoryName, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "Nativeness of Species Across Categories",
       y = "Species Category",
       fill = "Number of Species")

The heatmap shows how the nativeness of species varies across different categories. The largest combination is native vascular plants, with roughly 1200 species. Insects also have a large number of species, although many are classified as unknown, likely because determining the origin of many insect species can be difficult.

Across most categories, the majority of species appear to be native rather than non-native, suggesting that Yellowstone has maintained much of its natural ecological structure. Some categories contain unknown or NA values, which likely indicates that the nativeness of those species has not yet been classified, this is likely the case for Chromista as they are single celled aquatic organisms.

Overall, the heatmap suggests that most biodiversity within Yellowstone is composed of native species.

Plot 3: Native vs Non-Native Species by Category

ggplot(data = yellowstone_species, aes(x = CategoryName, fill = Nativeness)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(title = "Native vs Non-Native Species by Category",
      x = "Species Category",
      y = "Number of Species",
      fill = "Nativeness") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(na.value = "gray") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

The stacked bar plot provides a clearer view of the proportion of native versus non-native species within each category. Most categories are dominated by native species, with smaller proportions of non-native or unknown classifications.

One category that stands out is fish, which appears to have a relatively larger proportion of non-native species. This may be due to the fact that Yellowstone had a large number of trout introduced to support recreational fishing.

Overall, Yellowstone appears to maintain a strong majority of native species across most organism categories, which is important for preserving the natural balance of the park’s ecosystem.

Conclusion

Overall, the analysis shows that Yellowstone’s biodiversity is largely dominated by plants and insects, which make up the majority of recorded species in the park. Larger animal groups such as mammals represent a much smaller share of the total species count. Across most categories, the majority of species are native, with relatively small proportions of non-native species. Fish appear to have one of the higher shares of non-native species, which may be related to when many trout were introduced to Yellowstone.

One limitation of this analysis is that it focuses only on species counts. The data does not reflect population size, ecological impact, or how abundant each species actually is within the park. Because of this, some species may appear equally important in the data even though their real ecological roles differ.

With additional data or more time, a useful next step would be to incorporate variables such as abundance or find data on population estimates. This would allow for a deeper analysis of not just how many species exist in each category, but also how they contribute to the overall ecosystem and biodiversity of Yellowstone.

Connection to Class Ideas

The first visualization uses a lollipop chart to display the number of species within each category, as well as labeling the count for each category. Because the goal was to compare counts across several categories, the lollipop plot effectively highlights differences while keeping the visualization simple and uncluttered.

The second visualization uses a heatmap to examine the relationship between two categorical variables. Heatmaps are useful for identifying patterns across combinations of categories and allow viewers to quickly see where native, non-native, or unknown species are most common.

The third visualization uses a stacked proportional bar chart to show the composition of native versus non-native species within each category. Using proportions instead of raw counts makes it easier to compare categories that contain very different numbers of species. I kept NA in the second and third plots because they often appear in physically smaller categories, where the origin of the species may be more difficult to determine or where less research has been conducted.

Overall, these visualizations were intentionally designed to be simple and uncluttered to communicate patterns in the data. The goal was to present the information in a way that allows viewers to quickly interpret how biodiversity in Yellowstone is distributed across species categories and nativeness.

item.title: NFL Stadium Attendance
item.dc:creator: Cooper Olney
item.description:
Introduction

The data used in this analysis contains data on NFL stadium attendance, as well as time and day data on NFL games from the 2019 season (only games played during 2019) The dataset includes 299 observations, corresponding to the games played during this time period.

The variables I am most interested in are the weekly stadium attendance count which represents attendance for a single game, along with the day of week, time of day, and week within season the game took place. These variables provide insight into how attendance changes depending on when a game is played.

This leads to my primary question of interest:

How does NFL stadium attendance vary by day of the week, kickoff time, and week within the season

The data was accessed through the TidyTuesday project on a GitHub repository. The original source of the data is from Pro Football Reference.

Some additional context about the NFL is important for interpreting this data. The league consists of 32 teams across the United States, meaning some teams play in colder climates than others. Additionally, some teams play in indoor stadiums where outdoor weather doesn’t impact the fan experience. As the season progresses into November and December, teams in colder locations may experience a drop in attendance due to harsher weather conditions.

Games are typically played in one of three main time slots. One the east coast, these correspond roughly to 1:00pm (midday), 4:00pm (afternoon), and 8:00pm (primetime). The time a game starts could also affect attendance due to travel logistics, convenience, and how late the game ends. NFL games are usually played on Monday, Thursday or Sunday, with a few exceptions. This ties into kickoff time, as Monday and Thursday games are generally played during the primetime slot, so attendance may also be influenced by people’s work schedules or prior commitments.

Overall, these contextual factors motivate an exploration of how NFL stadium attendance is impacted by day of the week, kickoff time, and week within the season.

Primary Visualizations

Setting up the Data

library(tidyverse)
attendance <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-02-04/attendance.csv')
games <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-02-04/games.csv')
# Data Prep
games <- games |>
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week))

nfl_data <- games |>
  left_join(attendance, by = c("home_team_city" = "team",
                               "year" = "year",
                               "week" = "week")) |>
  filter(year == 2019) |>
  select(week, home_team, day, date, time, weekly_attendance) |>
  mutate(
    day = factor(day, levels = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")),
    date = mdy(paste0(date, ", ", 2019)),
    hour = hour(time),
    time_slot = case_when(
      hour <= 13.5 ~ "Midday",
      hour <= 17 ~ "Afternoon",
      hour >= 19 ~ "Primetime",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(time_slot)) |>
  mutate(time_slot = factor(time_slot, 
                            levels = c("Midday", "Afternoon", "Primetime")))

Plot 1: Mean NFL Stadium Attendance by Week

nfl_data |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarise(mean_attendance = mean(weekly_attendance, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = mean_attendance)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = week, xend = week, y = 0, yend = mean_attendance)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Mean NFL Stadium Attendance by Week",
    x = "Week of Season",
    y = "Average Attendance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

From the lollipop plot, we can see that during the 2019 NFL season, average stadium attendance did not vary substantially from week to week. It is interesting that the lowest average attendance was in week 6 at around 64,000 attendees, while the highest average attendance was in week 7 at around 69,000 attendees. Both of these weeks occurred during mid-October, and there are no obvious external factors that immediately explain why these two week are the furthest apart.

One possible explanation for the increase in attendance from week 6 to week 7 is variation in game quality. Week 7 may have featured more high profile matchups, stronger teams playing each other, or important rivalry games that attracted larger crowds.

Overall, the plot suggests that average NFL stadium attendance remains relativelty stable throughout the season, with only small flucutations from week to week.

Plot 2: NFL Stadium Attendance by Time Slot

ggplot(nfl_data, aes(x = time_slot, y = weekly_attendance, 
                     fill = time_slot)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "NFL Stadium Attendance by Time Slot",
    x = "Time Slot",
    y = "Weekly Attendance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

From the side-by-side boxplot, we can see that NFL stadium attendance was influenced by the game’s time slot during the 2019 season. The median attendance is higher for primetime games, which makes sense because the NFL typically schedules its most high profile matchups in the primetime slot. These games often feature stronger teams which are more likely to draw larger crowds. The midday time slot has the lowest median attendance. This also aligns with expectations, as lower profile games are generally scheudled during this window, which may lead to slightly smaller crowds.

Looking at the outliers and referencing the nfl_data dataframe, the high attendance outliers are primarily from the Dallas Cowboys as they have the largest stadium in the NFL by capacity. This naturally allows for higher attendance totals compared to other teams. On the lower end, the main outliers from the Los Angeles Chargers, who played their 2019 home games at a much smaller soccer stadium, as they were in the process of moving to a new permanent stadium. As a result, their attendance numbers were capped at a lower level than most other teams.

Overall, this plot suggests that kickoff time does have a noticeable relationship with attendance, with primetime games generally drawing the largest crowds.

Plot 3: NFL Stadium Attendance by Date, Day, and Time Slot

ggplot(nfl_data, aes(x = date, y = weekly_attendance, color = time_slot)) +
  geom_point() + 
  facet_wrap(~day, ncol = 1) +
  xlim(as.Date("2019-09-01"), as.Date("2020-01-05")) +
  labs(
    title = "NFL Stadium Attendance by Date, Day, and Time Slot",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Stadium Attendance",
    color = "Time Slot"
  )

This final plot examines how day of the week, time of day, and week within the season jointly relates to stadium attendance. Looking first at Monday games, all of them occur in the primetime slot. Attendance for these games generally falls between 60,000 and 80,00 attendees, reflecting the importance of Monday Night Football and the tendency to schedule high profile games during this time.

For Thursday games, most also take place during the primetime slot, with the exception of a few games in late November. These are the Thanksgiving Day games, which include an afternoon game. This games shows the highest attendance among Thursday games largely because it was hosted by the Dallas Cowboys, who have the largest stadium in the NFL, and it is a NFL tradition for the Cowboys to host a Thanksgiving game. There are also a small number of Saturday games, which tpyically occur late in the season once the college football regular season has finished. These games provide additional national viewing opportunities and tend to follow similar attendance patterns to Sunday games.

Sunday games make up the majority of the schedule and include games across all three time slots. Most Sunday games fall between 60,000 and 80,000 attendees, though there are some outliers due to differences in stadium capacity. Compared to weekday games, there are more games below 60,000 attendees largerly because many Sunday matchups are played in the midday and afternoon time slots, which tend to draw slightly smaller crowds on average.

Overall, across the full season, attendance appears relatively stable, with variations more strongly associated with time slot and stadium capacity than with the specific week of the season.

Conclusion

Overall, this analysis does not provide strong evidence that NFL stadium attendance varies substantially by week within the season. Average attendance appears relatively stable from week to week, suggesting that the timing within the season alone does not meaningfully impact how many fans attend games. There is, however, some evidence that attendance varies by time slot and day of the week. These two factors are closely related, as Monday and Thursday games are almost exclusively played in the primetime slot. Primetime games tend to show slightly higher attendance, which may be due to higher quality matchups, increased national attention, and scheduling that better fits fans’ work and personal commitments.

One limitation of this analysis is that it uses raw attendance counts rather than attendance as a percentage of stadium capacity. Stadium sizes vary significantly across the league. Because of these differences, attendance counts alone may reflect stadium capacity rather than true fan demand.

With additional data, a next step would be to incorporate each stadium’s maximum capacity and calculate an attendance rate. This would allow for a more meaningful comparison across teams and better isolate whether attendance truly changes by time of day, day of week, or week within the season. If attendance rate data were available, I would hypothesize that there would be greater variation later in the season compared to earlier weeks. Teams competing for playoff spots may experience sellout crowds, while teams that are no longer in contention may see reduced attendance. Using attendance rates instead of raw counts would make these differences easier to detect and interpret.

Connection to Class Ideas

The first plot uses a lollipop chart to display the mean attendance for each week of the season. Since my goal was to compare average attendance across weeks rather than examine the full distribution of values, a lollipop plot was an effective choice. It clearly emphasizes differences in means while minimizing visual clutter, making it easy to compare weeks side by side.

For the second plot, I used a side-by-side boxplot because it effectively displays the relationship between one quantitative variable (attendance) and one categorical variable (time slot). Boxplots are useful for comparing distributions, as they show the median, spread, and potential outliers within each group. This makes it easy to see how attendance differs across time slots. An unordered color palette was appropriate because time slot is a categorical variable without a numeric progression.

For the third plot, I faceted by the day and color coded by the time slot so that the plot was easier to read and so that viewers could see all the different variables at once. All the plots are intentionally simple, so viewers can quickly understand the patterns without being overwhelmed.

For the third plot, I used faceting by day of the week and color coding by time slot to allow viewers to examine multiple variables simultaneously. Both of these are effective ways to display multivariate relationships without overcrowding the plot. Overall, the plots were intentionally designed to be simple and uncluttered. By avoiding unnecessary complexity, the visualizations allow viewers to quickly interpret patterns in attendance without being overwhelmed by excessive detail.

item.title: Premier League Playing Style
item.dc:creator: Cooper Olney
item.description:
Introduction

The dataset used in this analysis contains English Premier League match data from the 2021-2022 season. The dataset includes 380 observations, corresponding to the 380 matches played over the course of a full season. Each match records performance statistics for both the home and away teams.

The variables I am most interested in are shots taken and fouls committed by the home and away teams. These variables provide insight into team playing styles, particularly whether home teams tend to play a more attacking style by generating more shots, and whether away teams are forced into a more defensive approach, potentially committing more fouls. Other metrics to also consider are corner kicks and yellow cards, as teams typically win more corners the more they attack, while yellow cards can indicate defensive play or time wasting tactics.

This leads to my primary question of interest:

Do home teams play a more attacking style of soccer, while away teams adopt a more defensive style of play?

This data was accessed through the TidyTuesday project on a GitHub repository. The original source of the data is from Evan Gower on Kaggle.

Some additional context about the Premier League is important for interpreting this data. The league consists of 20 teams, with each team playing 38 matches, once at home and once away against every other team. Match outcomes are scored as 3 points for a win, 1 point for a draw, and 0 points for a loss. Playing at home is widely believed to provide a competitive advantage due to factors such as crowd support, less traveling, better stadium amenities, and even differences in pitch dimensions.

As a result, teams often approach away matches more conservatively. Securing a draw away from home is typically considered a successful outcome, which encourages defensive strategies. In contrast, home matches are seen as opportunities to earn the maximum number of points, leading teams to adopt a more attacking style of play. Away teams may also attempt to slow the pace of the game through fouling or time-wasting, which can be reflected in higher foul counts and yellow cards.

Overall, these contextual factors motivate an exploration of whether match statistics such as shots taken and fouls committed support the commonly held belief that home teams attack more, while away teams defend more.

Primary Visualizations

Setting up the Data

library(tidyverse)
soccer <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2023/2023-04-04/soccer21-22.csv')
soccer <- soccer |> mutate(shot_diff = HS - AS,
                 foul_diff = HF - AF,
                 corner_diff = HC - AC)

Plot 1: Difference in Shots: Home vs Away

ggplot(data = soccer, aes(x = shot_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs( title = "Difference in Shots: Home vs Away", 
        x = "Home Shots − Away Shots", 
        y = "Number of Matches") +
  xlim(-29,29) +
  theme_minimal()

The distribution of the histogram is approximately normal, with its peak occurring when the home teams holds a 2-6 shot advantage. Looking at extreme shot differences, the home team out shooting the away team by 15 or more shots is more common than the other way around. This pattern suggests that home teams are generally more likely to play an attacking style of soccer. However, there is still a presence of negative values showing that matches end with the away team taking more shots. This indicates the home field advantage alone does not fully determine a team’s style of play, and that other factors such as overall team quality likely plays a role.

Plot 2: Difference in Fouls: Home vs Away

ggplot(data = soccer, aes(x = foul_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs( title = "Difference in Fouls: Home vs Away", 
        x = "Home Fouls − Away Fouls", 
        y = "Number of Matches") + 
  xlim(-20, 20) +
  theme_minimal()

The histogram peaks around a shot difference of 0, showing that in most matches there is little to no difference in the number of fouls committed by the home and away teams. However, the distribution is skewed to the left, with several negative outliers where the away team has committed many more fouls. This suggests that in certain matches, away teams are forced into a more defensive style of play, relying heavily on fouling to disrupt the home team’s attacks and slow the pace of the game.

Plot 3: Shot Difference by Match Outcome

ggplot(data = soccer, aes(x = FTR, y = shot_diff, fill = FTR)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + 
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("A" = "Away Win", "D" = "Draw", "H" = "Home Win")) +
  labs( title = "Shot Difference by Match Outcome", 
        x = "Final Match Result", 
        y = "Home Shots − Away Shots") + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  ylim(-29, 29) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  coord_flip()

The boxplots show a clear relationship between shot difference and the final match result. When the away team wins, the median shot difference is around -2, meaning that away victories typically occur when the away team is able to generate slightly more attacking opportunities than the home team.

For drawn matches, the median shot difference is about 2 suggesting that home teams still tend to take more shots even when the match ends level. Which is consistent with the idea that away teams often play more defensively and are satisfied with drawing matches away from home. When the home team wins, the median show difference rises to around 7, showing that home victories are strongly associated with attacking play style where the home team dominates the possession of the ball.

Overall, this plot supports the narrative that home teams generally play a more attacking style, while the away team adopts more defensive strategies. The plot also shows that the amount of attacking pressure a team can apply is potentially associated with the outcome of the match.

Conclusion

The analysis provides evidence that home teams tend to play a more attacking style and away teams adopt a more defensive approach, there are several limitations to consider in the analysis. Variables such as shots and fouls does not capture exactly how a team plays and all of the tactical decisions made during a match. Style of play can change based on differences in team quality, player injuries, or time in between the most recent match can all strongly influence how a team plays in the current match.

With additional data, a next step could be to incorporate team strength into the analysis. Teams could be grouped into upper, middle and lower tier categories based on where they finished in the Premier League table to find out how home field advantage interacts with overall talent. This could provide a deeper understanding of how playing style changes depending on venue. My hypothesis would be that middle tier teams would show the greatest change in style when switching between home and away matches.

Connection to Class Ideas

For the first two plots, I chose histograms because they effectively display a single quantitative variable, showing the center, shape, and spread of the data, as well as roughly how many observations there are in total. Since I was primarily interested in the distribution of the shot and foul differences, histograms made a lot of sense. The side-by-side boxplot works well for comparing a quantitative variable across a categorical variable, making it easy to see differences in distributions. I added color simply to make the plot visually appealing with an unordered color palette because a sequential or diverging color palette wasn’t needed in this case.

The plots are intentionally simple, so viewers can quickly understand the patterns without being overwhelmed. The dashed vertical lines highlight that positive differences correspond to the home team having more shots or fouls, and negative differences indicate the away team had more. I also set symmetric x-axis limits around zero to prevent skewed or inaccurate representations of the data, and to emphasize that the plot is split between home and away advantage. This ensures that zero remains central, reinforcing the narrative the half the plot represents a home advantage and the other half represents an away advantage.
